title: HTTP Methods and Status Codes
description: Understand how to use standard HTTP methods and return appropriate status codes so clients can reliably interpret API responses.

data.text: HTTP methods and status codes are the verbs and adjectives of your API. Methods describe the action the client wants to perform, while status codes describe the result of that action. Using them correctly makes your API predictable and easier to debug, test, and integrate with. Clients, monitoring tools, and load balancers all depend on these signals, so misuse can break automation and hide failures. A well-designed API uses the full HTTP vocabulary rather than reinventing it with custom headers or verbose error bodies.

GET retrieves a representation of a resource and should be safe and idempotent. POST creates a new subordinate resource or triggers a processing action. PUT replaces the entire resource with the request payload. PATCH applies partial updates to a resource. DELETE removes a resource. Each method maps to a specific intent, and clients rely on that contract when building integrations. Deviating from standard semantics forces every consumer to write custom logic instead of using standard HTTP libraries. This adds friction, increases bugs, and slows down the ecosystem around your API.

data.title: Idempotency Matters
data.text: Idempotent methods can be called multiple times with the same result. This matters for retries, network timeouts, and distributed systems where the same request might be delivered more than once.

Status codes are grouped into five classes. 2xx codes signal success. 3xx codes redirect or inform the client of further action. 4xx codes indicate client errors such as bad syntax or missing data. 5xx codes mean the server failed to fulfill a valid request. Using the most specific code available reduces ambiguity for API consumers and makes automated error handling possible. Generic codes like 500 or 400 hide the real problem and force clients to parse response bodies to understand what went wrong.

data.title: Status Codes in Practice
data.content: Return the most accurate status code for each operation.
data.code:
POST /orders
201 Created
Location: /orders/789

GET /orders/789
200 OK

GET /orders/9999
404 Not Found

POST /orders
400 Bad Request
{"error": "missing field: customerId"}

data.text: Beyond the basics, several status codes deserve special attention. 204 No Content is useful for successful deletes or actions with no body. 409 Conflict signals that the request could not be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the resource. 422 Unprocessable Entity is ideal for semantic validation failures where the syntax is correct but the business rules are violated. These finer distinctions help clients distinguish between different failure modes and recover appropriately, which is especially valuable in large distributed systems.

data.title: Status codes to know by heart
items: 200 OK — successful GET, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE.
201 Created — successful POST that created a resource.
204 No Content — successful DELETE or action with no body.
400 Bad Request — malformed syntax or invalid request body.
403 Forbidden — authenticated but not allowed to access.
404 Not Found — resource does not exist.
409 Conflict — request conflicts with current resource state.
500 Internal Server Error — unexpected server failure.

items.question: When should I use 422 instead of 400?
items.answer: Use 400 for syntactically invalid requests. Use 422 when the syntax is correct but the semantic content is invalid, such as failing business validation.

items.question: Should I return 200 for a failed POST?
items.answer: No. If the request failed, return the appropriate 4xx or 5xx code. 200 signals success to clients, load balancers, and monitoring tools.

data.title: Takeaway
points: Use standard methods for their intended operations.
Pick the most specific status code available.
Return machine-readable error bodies with 4xx and 5xx responses.
data.takeaway: Consistent use of methods and status codes turns your API into a self-documenting contract.
